findings.location: Results, paragraph 1 (confirmed identically in the PDF author manuscript, p. 8)
findings.quote: Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%).

consequence.explanation: Affects only the descriptive characterisation of EMA compliance as '70.00%'; no inferential result depends on it.

findings.notes: TOOL: computed by check_count_percent (MCP), which has no entry in this schema's technique enum; grim_percentage is its registered family and check_count_percent is documented as the strictly stronger sibling where the count is printed. The reproduction command names the actual verb. The paper's own numerator and denominator give 69.67%, not 70.00% -- a gap of 0.33 percentage points, and the printed value implies a denominator of ~4473 that appears nowhere in the paper. Two innocent explanations deserve weight: (1) compliance may have been computed as the MEAN of per-participant compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio, and those genuinely differ; (2) the authors may have rounded to a convenient figure. Against (2), the value is printed to two decimals, asserting four-significant-figure precision the pooled ratio does not support. I verified this is not an extraction or versioning artifact: the published XML prints '3131 out of 4494 ... (70.00%)' and the NIH author manuscript prints '3,131 out of 4,494 ... (70.00%)'. Both agree, so the discrepancy is the paper's. Note also 107 x 6 x 7 = 4494 exactly, so the denominator itself is internally correct.

findings.location: Table 1, BDI, CIA and DERS total-score rows

consequence.explanation: All three instrument totals are reachable as an integer sum over n = 107, so no descriptive value is impugned.

severity_source.note: check_table returned `suspicious` for these three cells. The GRIM granularity test itself PASSED on all three (grim_consistent: true); the only failing component was failure_mode 'out_of_range', which tests the implied sum against a 1-7 Likert maximum the tool DEFAULTED to because the paper states no scale range. A BDI, CIA or DERS total is not a 1-7 variable, so that range is an artifact of the default, bound_source was 'assumed', and rulebook rule 4 forbids resting a finding on a bound the paper never stated. Downgraded to `consistent` on the granularity dimension, which is the only dimension actually tested.

findings.notes: BDI 15.00 (10.00) is worth a reader's eye for a non-arithmetic reason: a mean of exactly 15.00 paired with an SD of exactly 10.00 is an unusually round combination. It is GRIM-consistent (15.00 x 107 = 1605 exactly), so nothing here is impossible; the likeliest innocent explanation is deliberate rounding to whole numbers in this one row. GRIMMER and SPRITE, which would test the SD, could not be run at all (see unchecked). Per the GRIM-family convention this awaits the editorial stage's R `scrutiny` cross-check, though as a `consistent` verdict it carries no accusation to confirm.

consequence.explanation: Every inferential claim the paper makes rests on a p-value that no reader can reconcile with its own point estimate and standard error.

findings.notes: TOOL: check_regression_batch (MCP), the batched form of check_regression. This is a refusal, not an accusation: nothing was checked, so nothing is confirmed and nothing is impugned. It is nonetheless the single largest verification gap in the paper. Table 2 prints b, SE, p and a standardised beta for all 84 paths but no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and no confidence interval anywhere, and the level-1 sample size (the number of momentary eating-episode observations) is never reported. Compounding this, b and SE are printed to two decimals, so even with df the implied Wald ratio for a row such as -0.07 (0.03) spans roughly 1.86 to 3.00 and pins p only to a range of about .003 to .063 -- a range that straddles .05. The printed precision is too coarse to adjudicate the paper's own significance decisions even in principle.

findings.notes: The interval was DERIVED (b +/- 1.96 x SE on the normal scale, no df being available); the paper prints no confidence interval, so this is not the authors' own interval and its bounds inherit the two-decimal rounding of b and SE. The point is not that the paper made an arithmetic error but that 'not significant' is being read as 'no association': the data remain compatible with an effect as large as 1.79 on the same scale on which the paper's significant between-person effects are 0.82 to 1.00. No smallest effect size of interest is stated anywhere in the paper, so equivalence cannot be assessed and no conclusion of absence is licensed by these numbers alone.

Computed from 1 result(s) significant uncorrected do not survive correction (a correction the paper did not apply, over a family we chose).

findings.notes: Deterministic arithmetic about the reported p-values, not an allegation: uncorrected testing across outcomes is ordinary in this literature. The family is my judgement -- six LOC eating dimensions crossed with two affect predictors, all measured on the same 107 participants for one stated hypothesis, which the rulebook treats as a single family. Surviving claims are a bound, 3 to 3 across all four methods; I quote Benjamini-Yekutieli (3 of 4 surviving) as the appropriate one because the six LOC dimensions are measured on the same people at the same moments and are certainly correlated. The three surviving everything (p = .001 each: general LOC, driven/compelled, disconnected) are robust to any correction. Note the paper also reports six further exploratory models in Data S1 testing the reverse direction on the same data, so the true comparison count exceeds 12 and this is a floor.

findings.notes: Of 12 between-person indirect effects, exactly one reaches p < .05 uncorrected, and it clears none of Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg or Benjamini-Yekutieli. Expected false positives under independence across this family is 0.6, of the same order as the single positive observed. Same caveats as the within-person family: family definition is my judgement, and correlated outcomes make the 46% family-wise error rate an upper bound rather than a point estimate. The paper states this result as a substantive conclusion ('participants who generally reported greater negative affect than other participants generally reported greater emotion dysregulation and, in turn, feeling more disconnected while eating throughout the study').

reported.published_xml_label: Positive affect ➜ Emotion dysregulation ➜ LOC eating

consequence.explanation: In the published version of record, six rows carrying the paper's central emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effects are labelled as a positive-affect mediation path, and that label duplicates a different row in the same model.

findings.notes: A production/versioning defect, not an arithmetic anomaly, and not evidence against the authors. In the published XML the third row of each model's 'Direct effects' block reads 'Positive affect to Emotion dysregulation to LOC eating' -- a three-term mediation path sitting under 'Direct effects', whose label is verbatim identical to a different row in the same model's 'Indirect effects' block carrying different numbers. Three independent lines of evidence establish the intended label is 'Emotion dysregulation to LOC eating': (1) the NIH author manuscript prints exactly that for the same rows and the same numbers; (2) the Results narrative describes these very values as the emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effect -- 'within-person (beta = 0.13-0.14) and between-person (beta = 0.68-0.77)' matches Models 1 and 6 exactly; (3) Figure 1's path diagram specifies this path. I read the PDF label from the page's TEXT layer, not from its inferred grid, which pdfplumber flagged grid_unreliable because the page is rotated. Worth flagging to the publisher: a reader of the version of record alone cannot correctly identify what six rows of the paper's central table report.

severity_source.note: The tool returned `indeterminate`; this finding records `suspicious`. A reason is stated in the finding.

findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text 'Results. Characteristics for the present sample (N = 107) are reported in Table 1. Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%).'

consequence.explanation: No APA-format test statistic exists to recompute, so statcheck's entire method is inapplicable to this paper.

findings.notes: Zero statistics found is the correct result, not a tool failure, and it carries information: the paper contains no t(df), F(df1,df2), r(df), chi-squared(df) or z anywhere in its prose. Its inferential content is expressed entirely as bare p-values and standardised betas in Table 2. The consequence is that the most standard automated consistency check in this toolkit cannot touch this paper at all -- the same underlying reporting gap as table2_coefficients_no_df, seen from a second direction.

findings.location: Participants and Procedures, first sentence of paragraph 2
findings.quote: The present study used baseline EMA data from a multisite randomized controlled trial (NCT0204349) testing the efficacy of Integrative Cognitive‐Affective Therapy (ICAT‐BED) versus guided self‐help Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Eating Disorders (CBTgsh).

consequence.explanation: The trial registration cannot be located from the identifier as printed, so a reader cannot check the parent trial's registered design or outcomes against this secondary analysis.

findings.notes: ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers are 'NCT' followed by eight digits; the printed string has seven, so it cannot resolve to any registration. No tool in this kit checks registry identifiers, so this is `manual` and capped at `suspicious`: no arithmetic was performed. I verified it by reading the string in both sources -- it appears identically in the published XML and on p. 6 of the author manuscript -- so it is a typographical error carried through production, not an extraction artifact. I have deliberately not guessed the intended number. This matters more than an ordinary typo because it sits in a load-bearing sentence: it is the paper's only pointer to the provenance and registered design of the data it analyses.

findings.location: Results, 'Emotion Dysregulation (M) to LOC Eating (Y)' paragraph, and Discussion, 'Variations Across LOC Eating Dimensions'
findings.quote: Specifically, there were significant positive associations between the emotion dysregulation factors relative to the general sense of LOC while eating and feelings of disconnection (e.g., numb, zoned out, on auto‐pilot) while eating factors at both the within‐person (β = 0.13–0.14) and between‐person (β = 0.68–0.77) levels.

computed.point_estimate_ordering: the 'non-significant' between-person coefficients (0.89, 0.85) are LARGER than the 'significant' one (0.82)

inputs.rows_compared: Table 2 Model 1 vs Model 3, between-person, direct and indirect

consequence.explanation: The paper's second stated aim -- that mediation 'varies across different LOC eating dimensions' -- is supported only by which side of alpha = .05 each separate test fell on, never by a test of the difference between dimensions.

findings.notes: No tool computed this; it is a reading of Table 2 against the paper's own conclusions, so it is `manual` and capped at `suspicious`. The headline claim of 'notable variations ... based on the LOC eating dimension' is drawn by comparing significance verdicts across six separately estimated models, and at the between-person level the contrast rests on p = .048 versus p = .055 -- with the point estimate of the NON-significant coefficient (0.89) larger than that of the significant one (0.82). This is the classic error of treating the difference between significant and non-significant as itself significant. The paper never reports a test of whether any two LOC dimensions differ, and since the six outcomes come from the same participants at the same moments, such a test is both possible and the appropriate way to support the claim. The Discussion nonetheless builds a substantive theoretical account on the contrast ('there may be certain stages of a LOC eating episode that may be precipitated by such a sequence'). The innocent reading is that this reflects conventional practice in the field rather than anything unusual to this paper; the consequence is that the novelty claim is weaker than stated.

findings.location: Figure 1, p. 19 of the author manuscript
findings.quote: Conceptual model depicting the associations of interest that were examined in the assessed multilevel structural equation models.

consequence.explanation: No statistic in this paper is reachable only through a figure, so the usual figure-blindness limitation does not apply here.

findings.notes: The paper's single figure is a path diagram with no axes and no plotted data -- it depicts model structure (lagging, levels, X/M/Y roles), not results. Recorded explicitly because 'we could not read the figures' is a standard caveat on these reviews and it is NOT a live gap for this paper: every number the paper reports is in its text or its two tables, all of which were read.

Table 2 (Multilevel structural equation models) - 84 coefficients (b, SE, p, beta) across 6 models x 2 levels; 71 submitted to regression-batch, all indeterminate for want of df; 21 rows cross-checked against the PDF

unchecked.location: Data S1 / Supplement (referenced 9 times; not provided to this review)
unchecked.reason: The largest coverage gap in this review. Data S1 is stated to contain: the model fit statistics for all six MSEMs (the basis of 'All MSEMs exhibited good fit'), the multilevel confirmatory factor analyses confirming the factor structure of affect, emotion dysregulation and LOC eating, the missing-data analyses that justify controlling for survey number, the comparison of the 5 excluded against the 107 retained participants, and the ENTIRE set of exploratory analyses. None of it could be read. 'Present but not supplied' is not the same as 'absent' -- no supplementary file was among the inputs for this paper.

An entire results section reports significance verdicts for a second set of six MSEMs ('indirect effects were significant for models involving momentary emotion dysregulation (predictor), negative affect (mediator), and four LOC eating dimensions') with no coefficient, no standard error and no p-value anywhere in the main text. Nothing in it is checkable. It also means the paper's true multiple-comparison count is at least double the 12 tests per family I could enumerate.

unchecked.location: Table 1, BDI, CIA and DERS total-score rows (GRIMMER and SPRITE)
unchecked.reason: check_table refused these three cells by design: GRIMMER and SPRITE need a STATED scale maximum and the paper gives none for any of the three instruments. Falling back on the tool's default 1-7 Likert range would manufacture an impossibility out of ordinary total scores. The SD of the BDI row (exactly 10.00, paired with a mean of exactly 15.00) is the one value in Table 1 I would most like to have tested and could not.

No degrees of freedom, no test statistic and no confidence interval are reported for any path, and the level-1 sample size (number of momentary eating-episode observations) is never given, so no reported p-value can be reconciled with its own b and SE. Additionally b and SE are printed to only two decimals, which for a coefficient such as -0.07 (0.03) leaves the implied p uncertain across a range that straddles .05.

unchecked.location: Results, paragraph 1, six LOC eating means and SDs
unchecked.reason: Six means and SDs are reported for the LOC eating dimensions with no n. The denominator is the number of surveys that followed an eating episode, which is never stated (it is a subset of the 3131 completed surveys). Without n, GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE cannot be run on any of them, even though these are single-item integer 1-5 responses and would otherwise be ideal candidates. Only the SD-range check, which needs no n, could be applied.

unchecked.location: Study Purpose, r = 0.948 between emotion dysregulation and negative urgency
unchecked.reason: Reported without n, df or confidence interval, and attributed to a prior analysis of the same sample (Wonderlich et al. 2024). It is within the logical bounds of a correlation, but no consistency check applies to a bare coefficient with no accompanying statistics. Worth noting substantively rather than forensically: at r = 0.948 this paper's mediator and the prior paper's mediator are very nearly the same variable.

The beta values cannot be independently verified against the unstandardised b without the latent factor variances at each level, which are not reported. They were read and recorded but no check was run on them.

Deliberately not run, and the reason matters. The paper has only ONE block of means and SDs (Table 1, a single sample), so there is no independent second block to compare against. In Table 2 the 'Negative affect to Emotion dysregulation' row repeats near-identically across all six models -- but this is EXPECTED, not duplication: the six models share the same predictor-to-mediator submodel on the same 107 participants and differ only in the outcome. Running the tool here would have flagged legitimate re-estimation as copy-paste. Supporting that reading, the between-person coefficient does vary across models (0.96, 0.96, 0.96, 0.95, 0.95, 0.95), exactly as re-estimation produces and copy-paste does not.

Not a finding, but recorded for the reader: data, materials and code are 'available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request' rather than deposited. This is an honest request-based statement rather than the 'all data are included' pattern rulebook rule 7 flags, but combined with the unavailable Data S1 it means none of the paper's fit statistics, factor analyses or exploratory results could be independently examined from published materials.
